sentences.text: The only known specimen preserves a pelvis that measures four centimeters in length.
A distinctive trait is a triangular depression located at the upper rear corner of the hip joint, which sits beneath a ridge.
The rear blade of the ilium forms a unique T-shape, terminating in an upward expansion longer than the blade's main shaft.
The fossilized bones display a porous texture called camellate bone, and every preserved vertebra contains internal air spaces.
Researchers inferred that the animal lacked teeth and likely possessed a crest on its snout based on its evolutionary relationships.
In November 2008, a four-year-old girl named Daisy Morris found the fossil remains at Atherfield Point on the Isle of Wight.
Paleontologist Martin Simpson verified the discovery in April 2009.
Darren Naish, Martin Simpson, and Gareth Dyke formally named the species Vectidraco daisymorrisae in a 2013 paper published in PLoS ONE to honor the young discoverer.
Initially, scientists placed Vectidraco in a basal position within Azhdarchoidea, suggesting it was one of the smallest members of that group.
Later studies in 2018 and 2020 reclassified the animal as a member of the family Tapejaridae, identifying it as a close relative to Tapejara and Europejara.
This creature lived between 125.77 and 119.57 million years ago, spanning the Barremian to Aptian stages.
The single known specimen dates to the early Aptian period and was found in the Chale Clay Member of the Atherfield Clay Formation.
